content: Decreased skin pigmentation can be categorized into two main types: hypopigmentation and depigmentation. Hypopigmentation refers to a reduction in skin pigment, while depigmentation indicates a complete loss of pigment. Differentiating between these two conditions is critical for establishing an accurate diagnosis, whether the condition is localized or generalized. Differential Diagnosis The potential causes of decreased skin pigmentation include the following conditions, listed alphabetically: Albinism: A genetic condition characterized by a lack of melanin production. Chemical leukoderma: Congenital birthmarks: Hypopigmented patches present at birth. Piebaldism: A rare genetic disorder resulting in patches of depigmented skin and hair. Pityriasis alba: A common skin condition causing hypopigmented, scaly patches, often seen in children. Tuberous sclerosis: A genetic disorder that can lead to hypopigmented macules among other systemic manifestations. Vitiligo: An autoimmune condition characterized by depigmented patches due to the destruction of melanocytes. Diagnosis History and Symptoms Assess the extent and severity of hypopigmentation or depigmentation. Investigate the patient’s family history for conditions such as thyroid disease, diabetes, or other endocrine disorders. Obtain a detailed personal medical history, including any history of allergies, hay fever, or asthma, as these may suggest an underlying diagnosis of atopic dermatitis. Eye Examination Conduct a thorough eye examination to assist in diagnosing albinism, as ocular findings are often present in this condition. Additional Diagnostic Tools Perform a Wood’s lamp examination to highlight areas of hypopigmentation or depigmentation, which may not be easily visible under normal lighting. Laboratory Findings In patients suspected of having vitiligo, a complete blood count (CBC) and thyroid function tests should be performed to evaluate for associated autoimmune conditions. Other Diagnostic Studies A skin biopsy may be necessary to confirm the diagnosis of vitiligo and to rule out other potential causes of depigmentation. Treatment Acute Pharmacotherapies for Vitiligo Topical corticosteroids are commonly used to manage vitiligo in its early stages. Chronic Pharmacotherapies for Vitiligo Oral beta-carotene supplementation may be beneficial for patients with chronic vitiligo or albinism to improve skin health and provide some photoprotection. Surgical Interventions In selected cases of vitiligo, punch minigrafting from areas of normal skin can be performed to help repopulate melanocytes in depigmented areas.
